questions_and_answers.question_text: How does jiàoyu differ in use from English "to educate"?
What are the two word orders for "not anymore"?
Which of the two is more emphatic?
What is the literal meaning of luànqībāzāo?
What does jìnbù mean as an adjectival verb in the PRC?

answers.answer_text: "To be (politically) progressive" — suited to the needs of the times and stimulating the development of society.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "I'm never coming back here again!"
What does luàn mean as an adverb?

answers.answer_text: "Arbitrarily, any old way, at random, indiscriminately."

questions_and_answers.question_text: Can luànqībāzāo be negated or used comparatively?

answers.answer_text: No — it is not made negative and is not used in comparative sentences.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "Don't write it just any old way."

articles.text:
3. A: Zuìjìn jǐnián jiàoyu gōngzuò   There's been a lot of progress in work
      yǒu hěn dàde jìnbù.            in education these past few years.
   B: Shì a, xuéxiàoli zài yě       Yes, schools aren't so messed up
      méiyou shénme luànqībāzāode    anymore.
      qíngkuàng le.

Notes on No. 3

jiàoyu: "to educate; education." Jiào is the same character as jiāo, "to teach," but in jiàoyu is pronounced with a FALLING tone. Yù means "to cultivate, to raise." Jiàoyu has some DIFFERENT USES from English "to educate." It is used not only for INSTITUTIONAL education but also for PARENTS' education of their children, and in the PRC for "education" of the people by the Communist Party.

Fùmǔ yīnggāi jiàoyu háizi nǔlì   Parents should teach their children
xuéxí.                           to study hard.
Jiātíng jiàoyu hé xuéxiào jiàoyu Education in the home is just as
yíyàng zhòngyào.                 important as school education.
Zhèiběn shū duì wǒ jiàoyu hěn dà. This book has educated me a lot.
                                 (PRC usage)

Another sense of jiàoyu is to try THROUGH REASON to convince a person to do things according to certain rules:

Nǐ děi jiàoyu jiàoyu nǐde háizi. You have to try to straighten out
                                 your child.

jìnbù: "to make progress, to advance"; as a noun, "progress." Literally "to put forward steps."

Tāde Zhōngwén jìnbù tài màn.     His Chinese is progressing too slowly.

Jìnbù is commonly used with the verb yǒu, especially yǒu hěn dàde jìnbù.

In the PRC, jìnbù is used as an ADJECTIVAL verb meaning "to be (politically) PROGRESSIVE."

zài yě méiyou...le: "not anymore." The adverb zài and a negative can express not doing something anymore. There are TWO WORD ORDERS:

     méiyou              (yě) méiyou
zài            OR   zài
     bù                  (yě) bù

The SECOND pattern is MORE EMPHATIC. Zài should be given SPECIAL STRESS:

Wǒ ZÀI bù huílai le!             I'm never coming back here again!
Wǒ ZÀI yě bù chī táng le.        I'm never going to eat candy again.

luàn: "to be in disorder, to be in a mess, to be chaotic"

Zhèr tài luàn.                   It's too chaotic (noisy) in here.
Tāde zhuōzishang zǒng shi hěn    His table top is always a mess.
luàn.

As an ADVERB, luàn means "arbitrarily, any old way, at random, indiscriminately."

Bú yào luàn xiě.                 Don't write it just any old way.
Bú yào luàn pǎo.                 Quit running all over the place.

luànqībāzāo: "to be in disorder, to be in a mess," literally "chaotic-seven-eight-rotten." Some have translated this as "at sixes and sevens." It can refer to PHYSICAL or MORAL messes.

Duìbuqǐ, fángjiān luànqībāzāode. I'm sorry, the room is a mess.

Luànqībāzāo is NOT made negative and is NOT used in comparative sentences.
